questions.question: Explain why mining at Kimberley moved underground and how this changed the work.
questions.expected_answer: In the early 1870s the mines were open pits of many small claims, with ground hauled up by ropes and buckets. As they deepened, the weathered reef on the sides collapsed in reef falls, burying claims and killing workers, and water flooded the bottom. By the early 1880s the Kimberley Mine was over 100 metres deep. From about 1885, shafts were sunk in solid rock outside the pit and tunnels driven into the blue ground, which was blasted, hauled in trucks and lifted by steam winding engines. This needed large capital for engines, pumps, rails and explosives, so only large companies could mine, leading to consolidation into De Beers in 1888. Work changed from small groups on claims to large gangs underground under white overseers, at a pace set by machines and the company. The Witwatersrand followed on a larger scale because the gold reefs sloped deep underground.

questions.question: Describe the dangers and health risks faced by miners underground.
questions.expected_answer: Rockfalls were the commonest cause of death, as blasting and rock pressure brought down roofs despite timber props. Explosives were dangerous, especially misfires struck later by drills, and fumes filled tunnels. Fire in timbered tunnels was deadly: the De Beers Mine fire of 11 July 1888 killed about 200 miners, mostly black workers trapped deep in the mine. Deep mines were hot and humid, poorly ventilated, dark and lit by candles, with shifts of ten or more hours and long ladders and walks. Dust from drilling caused silicosis, or miners' phthisis, especially on the quartz-rich gold mines, raising the risk of tuberculosis; pneumonia killed many, especially workers moving from hot mines into cold highveld nights and recruits from tropical regions; poor compound food caused scurvy. Death rates were very high.

questions.question: Explain how work and treatment underground were divided by race.
questions.expected_answer: Black migrant workers did the heavy manual work: hand drilling, lashing or shovelling broken rock, pushing trucks and timbering. White workers were skilled tradesmen such as engine drivers, fitters and blasters, and supervisors and overseers of black gangs. This division was protected by custom and later by law as the colour bar, reserving certain jobs for white workers regardless of black workers' experience; the Mines and Works Act of 1911 gave it legal force on the mines. White workers earned many times more, lived with families in town, had the vote and could form unions; black workers were on contracts in compounds, without votes or recognised unions, and received much smaller compensation, if any, for injury or death, many being sent home when injured.
